newsitem.title: USA: Christian Coalition vows to work for blacks.
newsitem.headline: Christian Coalition vows to work for blacks.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
The Christian Coalition, an overwhelmingly white, evangelical, conservative force in U.S. politics, said Thursday it was changing direction and wanted to embrace blacks and Hispanics.
The Coalition, which claims 1.7 members and a network of 100,000 churches, announced a new programme intended to combat poverty and revitalise American inner city ghettoes.

"For too long, our movement has been primarily and frankly almost exclusively a white, evangelical, Republican movement whose centre of gravity has rested in the cloistered safety of the suburbs," said Coalition director Ralph Reed.

"Today, we propose a bold plan that shatters the colour line and bridges the gap that has separated white evangelicals and Roman Catholics from our African-American and Latino brothers and sisters," he said.

In recent years, the Coalition has emerged as a key power centre in the Republican Party. Two years ago, when he presented his legislative programme for the last Congress, Reed was flanked by top Republicans, including House Speaker Newt Gingrich and then Senate Majority Leader Bob Dole.
This time, Reed was joined by a collection of black and Hispanic church pastors. There were no politicians on hand.

The programme, called the "Samaritan Project," included proposals to provide government-financed scholarships for low income children in 100 of the country's worst school districts to attend private schools. It also proposed a $500 tax credit for people giving money and at least 10 hours of their time to private charitable organisations that served the poor.
The Coalition also backed the idea of establishing so-called empowerment zones in inner cities with tax breaks for individuals starting small businesses.

In a declaration of distance from the Republicans, Reed said the Christian Coalition disagreed with the party's support for legalised gambling, which he said was taking money away from the poor and giving it to the rich "on the basis of a cheat and a lie."

Reed's new programme was greeted unenthusiastically by at least one liberal organisation, People for the American Way, whose president Carole Shields said it was nothing more than a scheme to channel public money to religious institutions.
"When the Christian Coalition talks about helping the poor, it always leads to moving tax dollars to religious institutions," Shields said.
She said the school scholarship idea would allow a handful of the nation's school districts to use tax dollars for private schools, many of which were church schools.

Reed said the Coalition was not abandoning its traditional agenda, including its uncompromising opposition to abortion. But he said the organisation was changing and wanted to acknowledge past mistakes, particularly its failure to adequately address racial issues.
